lessons.title: Vertices, edges and adjacency
lessons.description: A vertex represents a distinct object and an edge represents a relationship between two objects. Adjacency lists give each vertex its neighbors; adjacency matrices use a cell for every possible pair.
lessons.analogy: For a supplier graph, represent suppliers, components and factories as nodes; label each edge supplies or usedBy. Compare a list lookup with a matrix lookup.
learn: Explain vertices, edges and adjacency precisely and identify its assumptions.

Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: For a supplier graph, represent suppliers, components and factories as nodes; label each edge supplies or usedBy. Compare a list lookup with a matrix lookup.
Design a negative test based on: Do not infer that an undirected supplier link means the same as a directed supply chain dependency.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes vertices, edges and adjacency?
options: More connections always prove a more accurate knowledge graph.
A vertex represents a distinct object and an edge represents a relationship between two objects. Adjacency lists give each vertex its neighbors; adjacency matrices use a cell for every possible pair.
Any result is valid if the UI displays a graph.
quiz.why: A vertex represents a distinct object and an edge represents a relationship between two objects. Adjacency lists give each vertex its neighbors; adjacency matrices use a cell for every possible pair. Key failure: Do not infer that an undirected supplier link means the same as a directed supply chain dependency.

lessons.try: Practice: For a supplier graph, represent suppliers, components and factories as nodes; label each edge supplies or usedBy. Compare a list lookup with a matrix lookup. Write down what changes when an edge is reversed, removed, or made stale.

lessons.title: Directed and undirected graphs
lessons.description: A directed edge (u,v) is ordered, while an undirected {u,v} permits symmetric traversal. A digraph may have incoming and outgoing degrees; symmetry must not be assumed.
lessons.analogy: Represent purchasesFrom as directed while physicallyConnectedTo may be undirected. Reverse both edges to see which business claims become false.
learn: Explain directed and undirected graphs precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Represent purchasesFrom as directed while physicallyConnectedTo may be undirected. Reverse both edges to see which business claims become false.
Design a negative test based on: Do not automatically reverse owns, produces, or reportsTo relationships.

lessons.title: Weighted edges and cost models
lessons.description: A weighted graph attaches a numeric cost to each edge. The choice of units and aggregation policy determines the meaning of an optimal path.
lessons.analogy: For a logistics network use transit hours on lanes; add delays along a path and compare total time, not hop count.
learn: Explain weighted edges and cost models precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: For a logistics network use transit hours on lanes; add delays along a path and compare total time, not hop count.
Design a negative test based on: Mixing currencies, kilometers, hours, and similarity scores without normalization produces meaningless paths.

lessons.title: Walks, trails, paths and cycles
lessons.description: A walk may repeat vertices and edges; a trail cannot repeat an edge; a simple path cannot repeat vertices. A cycle returns to its start under graph-specific definitions.
lessons.analogy: Trace service A → B → C → A; identify the cycle and explain why deployments may oscillate.
learn: Explain walks, trails, paths and cycles precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Trace service A → B → C → A; identify the cycle and explain why deployments may oscillate.
Design a negative test based on: Calling all traversals shortest paths hides cycles and revisits.

lessons.title: Degree, in-degree and out-degree
lessons.description: Degree counts incident edges; in-degree and out-degree distinguish incoming and outgoing connections in directed graphs. Degree is local, not a measure of global influence.
lessons.analogy: Count downstream assets from a data product and upstream feeds into it; interpret in-degree versus out-degree.
learn: Explain degree, in-degree and out-degree precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Count downstream assets from a data product and upstream feeds into it; interpret in-degree versus out-degree.
Design a negative test based on: High degree does not imply authority, correctness, or operational criticality.

Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Remove the integration between two regional catalogs and count resulting weak components.
Design a negative test based on: An undirected component count does not prove two nodes are reachable in the required direction.

learn: Explain trees, dags and dependency graphs precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Create a data-pipeline DAG and choose a valid build order. Add A→B→A and watch topological ordering fail.
Design a negative test based on: Treating an arbitrary RDF knowledge graph as a tree drops legitimate cross-links.

lessons.description: A bipartite graph partitions vertices into two groups such that edges go between groups. Multipartite graph designs generalize to more typed sets.

learn: Explain bipartite and multipartite graphs precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Construct Customers ↔ Products purchases; use a projection to compare co-purchased products.
Design a negative test based on: Projecting bipartite relationships can create dense links that were never direct facts.

lessons.title: Multigraphs, hypergraphs and reification
lessons.description: A multigraph permits multiple edges between a pair of vertices. A hypergraph connects sets of vertices; RDF statement-level metadata often uses RDF-star where supported or explicit event nodes.
lessons.analogy: Record two separate supplier contracts between the same companies with different effective periods.
learn: Explain multigraphs, hypergraphs and reification precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Record two separate supplier contracts between the same companies with different effective periods.
Design a negative test based on: Collapsing parallel statements loses contract identity and provenance.

lessons.title: Graph density and sparsity
lessons.description: For a simple undirected graph with n vertices, density is 2m/(n(n−1)); for a simple directed graph without loops it is m/(n(n−1)). Real enterprise graphs are often sparse.
lessons.analogy: Compare 12 nodes and 15 links with a complete graph of 66 links; discuss UI clutter versus information.
learn: Explain graph density and sparsity precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Compare 12 nodes and 15 links with a complete graph of 66 links; discuss UI clutter versus information.
Design a negative test based on: Density formula assumptions break for parallel edges, self loops, and mixed graph types.

lessons.title: Subgraphs and induced neighborhoods
lessons.description: A subgraph uses a subset of vertices and edges. An induced subgraph includes all existing edges among its chosen vertices; k-hop neighborhoods bound exploration depth.

learn: Explain subgraphs and induced neighborhoods precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Inspect all dependencies within two hops of a critical system before drawing the whole enterprise graph.
Design a negative test based on: A filtered graph view is not deletion from the underlying model.

lessons.title: Graph representation, serialization and identity
lessons.description: An in-memory graph may use adjacency lists, tables or triples; RDF graph statements preserve predicates and IRIs; property graphs attach labels and properties. Mappings require explicit policies.

lessons.title: Breadth-first search and minimum hops
lessons.description: Breadth-first search explores an unweighted graph in layers from a source. A FIFO queue discovers the fewest-edge route when all edges have equal cost.
lessons.analogy: From an incident node trace the minimum number of dependency edges to a customer-facing API.
learn: Explain breadth-first search and minimum hops precisely and identify its assumptions.
Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: From an incident node trace the minimum number of dependency edges to a customer-facing API.
Design a negative test based on: BFS minimizes edge count, not travel time, severity or cost.

lessons.title: Dijkstra shortest weighted path
lessons.description: Dijkstra calculates shortest paths when edge weights are nonnegative. It repeatedly settles the least-cost tentative distance, typically using a priority queue.

Apply the concept to this enterprise scenario: Select the fastest transport route from a parts supplier to a plant using positive hour estimates.
Design a negative test based on: Negative weights invalidate Dijkstra; stale cost weights may mislead operational routing.

learn: Explain bellman–ford and negative edges precisely and identify its assumptions.
